note.question: How should a ride-hailing platform price solo and shared trips when riders’ decentralized choices jointly determine congestion, pairing delays, market size, and the platform’s objective?
note.overview: A platform first sets solo and shared prices; self-interested riders then choose whether to join and which service to use while anticipating the congestion and pairing effects created by other riders. The paper explicitly solves this Stackelberg queueing game.

source.quote: We consider the operations of a ride-hailing platform in a designated region (e.g., an airport ride-hailing pickup zone).
Below, we describe the modeling details of riders, drivers, and rider-driver matching in turn.

An interesting dynamic is that customers’ adoption of the low-quality service (i.e., shared rides) can improve not only the quality of this service, but also the quality of the high-end service (i.e., solo rides) by producing shorter wait times, and this happens in three ways: boosting the system’s utilizable capacity, moderating the variability of customer in-flow, and curtailing cus­ tomers’ pair-up time.

models.method: The authors solve a two-dimensional Markov chain for stationary solo and shared wait times, derive rider discomfort cutoffs and joining equilibria, transform platform price choices into induced market outcomes, compare three objectives analytically, and calibrate the model to Chicago data.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: In stage 1 the platform posts solo price p_1 and shared price p_2 for one of three objectives. In stage 2 riders arrive, use long-run queue statistics, and simultaneously determine an equilibrium joining rate and sharing fraction; drivers arrive exogenously in the base model and serve the virtual queue first come, first served. A shared trip consumes one driver for two riders but adds partner-pairing delay and discomfort. More sharing reduces system load and can shorten both shared and solo waits.
